title: Your Life As Every CIA Black Ops Rank
hook: By the time this ends, the CIA will officially deny you ever existed. Somewhere right now, someone is signing up for that deal without knowing it.

levels.name: The Applicant
beats: You apply online like everyone else. There's a form on the CIA website. You fill in your name, your education, your work history. You click submit and wait.
6 months later, you get an email. They want to interview you. You fly to Virginia on your own dime.
The building looks like any other government office. Fluorescent lights, bad coffee, a man in a gray suit. 4 hours of questions.
Where did you grow up? What languages do you speak? Have you ever used drugs? Have you ever been arrested?
The questions seem random, but they're not. They're building a profile, looking for patterns, looking for lies. You pass the interview. Then comes the polygraph.
The strap tightens across your chest. Two sensors clip to your fingers. A blood pressure cuff squeezes your left arm until your hand starts to tingle.
The room is small, white walls, fluorescent light, no windows. The only things inside are you, a chair, and a man whose face gives away nothing.
Have you ever committed a crime you weren't caught for? Your heart rate spikes and the machine records it. Your breathing shifts and the machine records that too.
The machine cannot actually detect lies. It measures stress, arousal, discomfort, but it cannot distinguish between a liar and a nervous person telling the truth. You don't know that yet.

And because you don't know, you confess. Small things, stupid things, things you buried so deep you forgot they were there. You confess because the machine feels omniscient and the man behind it never blinks.
3 weeks later, a letter arrives. You've been accepted into the clandestine service trainee program. Welcome to the CIA.

levels.name: The Trainee
beats: They send you to Camp Perry, Virginia. The locals call it the farm. It's 9,000 acres of woods, swamps, and training facilities surrounded by fences topped with razor wire and armed guards at every gate.
Officially, it's a Department of Defense research facility. Unofficially, for the next 18 months, this is your home.

At 5 in the morning, your feet hit the ground before your brain catches up. A five-mile run through Virginia fog so thick you can taste the moisture in it, followed by breakfast that's fast, silent, and functional.
You sit in classrooms learning about foreign governments, terrorist organizations, and intelligence tradecraft. Tradecraft is the CIA's word for spy skills.
You learn how to spot surveillance. A car that's been behind you for three turns. A woman reading a newspaper who glanced at you twice. A man at the cafe whose coffee hasn't moved in 40 minutes.

You learn how to disappear. You duck into a department store through the ground floor, take the escalator to the third floor, move through women's clothing, past the fitting rooms, down the service corridor, and out through the loading dock.
A car is waiting with the engine running. 30 seconds later, you're gone. The tail is still circling the block.
You learn lockpicking on embassy grade deadbolts, safe cracking on government vaults, how to plant a listening device in a room you were never supposed to enter and leave no evidence you were there.
How to photograph a classified document in 4 seconds flat and slide it back into the folder as though nothing happened.
Then comes the part they don't put in the recruitment materials. You learn how to recruit assets, which is their word for convincing people to betray their countries.
You study psychology, manipulation, persuasion. You learn the four motivations: money, ideology, coercion, and ego. MICE. Everyone fits into one of these categories.
You run practice operations in nearby cities. Richmond, Norfolk, Washington. Your instructors play the role of foreign intelligence officers trying to catch you.
If they catch you, you fail. If you fail too many times, you're out. The washout rate is 40 percent.
Some people crack under the pressure. Some can't handle the deception. Some buckle under psychological exercises that include sleep deprivation, staged interrogations, and 72 hours of gaslighting.

The ones who survive aren't necessarily the smartest or the strongest. They're the ones who can compartmentalize, who can do something terrible at 9 in the morning and sit down to dinner with their families at 6 as though nothing happened.
They're the ones who can build a wall between who they are and what they do and never let anyone see where the door is.
You graduate in the top 15 percent of your class. They give you a badge and a cover identity. You are now a CIA operations officer. Your real career is about to begin.

levels.name: The Case Officer
beats: Your first posting is an embassy in Eastern Europe, a former Soviet bloc country where the walls still carry the memory of who built them. Officially, you're a political attache, your name on a diplomatic list.
You attend diplomatic functions in uncomfortable suits, making small talk with people you're secretly evaluating as potential targets. Unofficially, you're a spy.
Every handshake at every reception is an evaluation. Every conversation over warm champagne and cold canapes is an interview the other person doesn't know they're having.
You scan the room, running four calculations at once. Who has access? Who has weakness? Who has motive? Who can be turned?
You study targets the way a surgeon studies an X-ray, examining habits, routines, debts, addictions, family problems, political frustrations. Everyone has a mechanism. Everyone can be opened.
Your first recruitment takes eight months. He's a mid-level bureaucrat in the foreign ministry. He has access to diplomatic cables. He has gambling debts.
You approach him at a casino. You buy him drinks. You become his friend. You loan him money to cover his losses. Then you loan him more. Then more.
By month six, the loans total $50,000, a manufactured dependency constructed cent by cent. He cannot repay it. He knows it. You know it. Neither of you says it aloud.
By month eight, you ask him for a favor. Just a few documents. Internal memos. Nothing important. Or so you tell him. And so he tells himself.
He agrees. He has no real choice. He's been agreeing for months without recognizing it.
You now have an asset inside the foreign ministry. You eat dinner at the embassy that night and feel nothing in particular.

levels.name: The NOC
beats: Most CIA officers work under official cover. They're diplomats or military attaches with badges, offices in the embassy, and diplomatic immunity. If they get caught, they get expelled from the country. Embarrassing, but not dangerous.
You're offered something different. Non-official cover. NOC, pronounced knock. The most dangerous job in the intelligence community.
You won't have diplomatic protection. You won't have an embassy to run to. No badge, no government ID, nothing connecting you to the United States government.
If you get caught, you're on your own. The CIA will deny you exist. The State Department will deny you exist. The president will deny you exist.
You'll be prosecuted under local laws. In some countries, that means prison. In others, torture. In others, a bullet in the back of the head and an unmarked grave. You say yes.
They build you a legend, their word for a fake identity. You're now a businessman. You work for a consulting firm that doesn't actually do any consulting.
It's a CIA front company with real offices, real employees, real clients. None of them know who you really are.
You live your cover 24 hours a day. Your neighbors think you're a management consultant. Your girlfriend thinks you travel for work. Your parents think you quit the government years ago.

The only people who know the truth are your handlers back at Langley. All communication goes through dead drops. A chalk mark on a wall. A package taped under a park bench. An encrypted message buried in the code of an ordinary-looking website.
You sleep with a packed bag and a passport, not yours, under the mattress. You check every reflection and every window for the face that appears too often.
You memorize the vehicles behind you, vary your route home every single day, and never use the same cafe twice in the same month.

You are operationally, existentially, structurally alone. There is no one on Earth who knows both your real name and your current location. If you die tonight, the truth of who you were dies with you.

levels.name: The Paramilitary Officer
beats: They pull you out of NOC work after your cover is almost blown in Beirut. A local intelligence service got suspicious. Two men in a parked car that shouldn't be there. A woman on the third floor with a camera lens that catches the light for half a second.
Your cover is compromised. Not fully exposed, but the fracture exists, and fractures only widen.
They extract you, debrief you for three weeks in a windowless room in Virginia, and present you with a new path. The Special Activities Division, SAD.
This isn't about deception anymore. This is about direct action. You go through another round of training. Six months of the most intense military training on the planet.
Small unit tactics, close quarters combat, explosives and demolitions, advanced weapons training, high altitude parachute operations, free falling from 30,000 feet.
Combat diving, SERE, survival, evasion, resistance, and escape, where they confine you in a box for days to teach you what captivity feels like before it happens for real.

Most of your instructors are former Delta Force or SEAL Team Six. They don't care about your recruitment skills. They care about whether you can kick down a door and clear a room without getting your team killed.
Your first mission is in Afghanistan. You spend three months in a mud compound in a valley that doesn't appear on any official map.
You grow a beard and wear local clothes. You eat what the local militia fighters eat: flatbread, rice, and goat.
The men you work alongside have fought for decades. Their loyalties are fluid. The only constant is that everyone has a price.
Your job is to locate targets and eliminate them. You watch through binoculars as hellfire missiles turn buildings into craters.

Sometimes the intelligence is accurate. Sometimes the intelligence is wrong. The target isn't there. Families eating dinner in the wrong building at the wrong time because a grid coordinate was off by 200 meters.
You try not to think about the times it goes wrong. You have another mission tomorrow.
They award you a medal that doesn't have a name. The ceremony has no official record. The mission it recognizes never officially occurred in a country where you were never officially present.

levels.name: The Team Leader
beats: After five years in SAD, you're promoted to team leader. You run your own unit, eight operators. You're responsible for the mission. You're responsible for their lives.
Your team is deployed to Libya following the collapse of the regime. The country is disintegrating. Militias occupy every city. Weapons depots are looted. Armed groups answer to no one.
Your mission is to locate and secure chemical weapons before they fall into the wrong hands. Any group that would love to have mustard gas or sarin.
Six weeks in Tripoli while the city burns around you. You operate at night, sleep two hours at a time in safe houses that change every 48 hours.

You bribe militia commanders for information. You interrogate prisoners whose accounts change with each telling. You pay informants who might be lying, might be setting you up, might be working for three factions simultaneously.
You find three caches of mustard gas that the official reports said didn't exist. 15 tons of chemical weapons.
You destroy them in place, rig explosives, and incinerate everything. The smoke rises thick and black, and you hope the wind doesn't shift.
On your last night in country, your convoy is ambushed. A side street, muzzle fire. One of your men goes down, then another.
You carry one of them half a mile to the extraction point while rounds snap past your head. The helicopter arrives. You get out. One survives, the other doesn't.
You write letters to their families using words like service and sacrifice and grateful nation. You don't mention Tripoli, the mustard gas, the side street, or the half-mile carry.
The letters are composed of omissions, and the families frame them.

levels.name: The Station Chief
beats: You've been in the field for 15 years. Your body is breaking down. A shoulder that dislocates, Afghanistan. Knees that grind every morning, too many parachute landings.
Permanent ringing in your left ear, an explosion in a country you're not permitted to name. You're 42 years old and you feel 60.
They make you chief of station, COS, the senior CIA officer in an entire country. Every operation, every asset, every piece of intelligence flows through you.
You manage 40 officers and hundreds of local assets. You meet with the ambassador every morning.
You meet with local intelligence services, some allies, some adversaries pretending to be allies, some assets you recruited years ago who are now running their own services.
You approve operations that could start international incidents. You kill operations that carry too much risk. Every decision is a gamble.
Every success is classified. Every failure ends up on the front page. You sleep four hours a night.
Your marriage ended during your second tour in the Middle East. Your kids are grown now. They know the cover story. They know the person you pretend to be.

levels.name: The Black Site Commander
beats: They need someone to run a facility that doesn't exist, a black site, in a country that will deny it's there. Inside there are cells.
The prisoners are high value detainees, terrorist leaders, bomb makers, financiers, couriers. They were captured in raids across a dozen countries.
Never formally arrested, never appeared before a judge, no lawyers, no rights, no official existence. As far as the world knows, they vanished.
Your job is to extract intelligence from them. Enhanced interrogation, a phrase designed by lawyers to occupy the space between what the law prohibits and what the government requires.
Sleep deprivation lasting 72 hours or more. Stress positions held until muscles fail, and then held longer.
Waterboarding. A cloth over the face, water poured until the body believes it's drowning.
Some of these techniques were legal when you started using them. Some were made legal retroactively by memos written in offices with pleasant views and good coffee.
You tell yourself it's necessary. You tell yourself the information saves lives. On some nights, you believe it.
On other nights, you lie awake, uncertain whether you're still among the people doing the right thing, or whether that distinction stopped carrying meaning a long time ago.
You run the facility for two years. When you leave, they give you a commendation that will never appear in any record.

levels.name: The Division Director
beats: You're back at Langley, the building you first entered 25 years ago as a nervous applicant. You walk past the memorial wall every morning.
139 stars carved into white marble. No names beside them. Some belong to colleagues. Some belong to friends.
You run an entire division of the National Clandestine Service. Hundreds of officers report to you. Thousands of assets worldwide feed information into your systems.
Billions of dollars in black budget funding flow through your accounts. Money that officially doesn't exist.
You brief the president on covert operations. You sit in the situation room with the secretary of defense and the national security adviser.
You recommend targets for drone strikes. You authorize operations in countries where the government is not officially operating.
You testify before congressional intelligence committees. The real briefings happen in closed sessions with no transcripts.
The senators ask questions. You give answers that are technically true but carefully incomplete. They don't want the details. They want plausible deniability. You give it to them.
The whole thing is a machine that runs on secrets and blood, and you're one of the people who keeps it running.

levels.name: The Ghost
beats: You retire after 30 years. There's a small ceremony in a conference room at Langley. 50 people attend.
The director gives a speech about sacrifice and dedication and the price of freedom. Your colleagues applaud. Some of them are crying.

You receive the Distinguished Intelligence Cross, the highest award the CIA can give. It will sit in a box in your closet because you can't display it. If someone discovers it, you'll say it's a replica.
You sign more non-disclosure agreements. Everything you did, everything you saw, everything you know is classified for the rest of your life. The truth of your career is a felony to speak aloud.
You move to a house in Virginia, far from the city. You don't have many friends. The people you worked with are scattered or dead.

You can't explain the scars. You can't explain why you check the locks three times before going to bed. You can't explain why you wake up at 3 in the morning and walk the perimeter looking for threats that aren't there.
Your pension is generous. Your healthcare is excellent, but you're alone with your memories. The assets who were caught and executed. The operations that went wrong.
None of it officially happened. None of it will ever be acknowledged. You are a ghost.
And when you die, there will be a star on a wall at Langley. No name, just a star. One more anonymous sacrifice in a war that never ends.
Somewhere at this moment, a young person is filling out an application on the CIA website, sitting in a college dorm room, dreaming of adventure, dreaming of serving their country.

They have no idea what they're really signing up for. They don't know about the polygraph, the farm, the asset with the gambling debts, the letters composed of omissions, the black site, the box in the closet, or the star with no name.
They don't know that this job will hollow them out and fill them back up with secrets. But they'll learn. They always do.
